A standard chessboard has **64** squares if you count only the individual light and dark squares. If you count every square that can be traced on the board, including larger squares made up of smaller ones, the answer is **204**.

## Counting squares of every size

In addition to the 1 × 1 squares, the 8 × 8 grid contains 2 × 2 squares, 3 × 3 squares, and so on, up to the entire board, which is itself one 8 × 8 square. The key is to count how many positions each size can occupy.

Take a 2 × 2 square. Its top-left corner can sit in any of the first 7 columns and any of the first 7 rows, so there are 7 × 7 = 49 of them. In general, a k × k square fits in (9 − k)² positions:

| Square size | How many |
|---|---|
| 1 × 1 | 8² = 64 |
| 2 × 2 | 7² = 49 |
| 3 × 3 | 6² = 36 |
| 4 × 4 | 5² = 25 |
| 5 × 5 | 4² = 16 |
| 6 × 6 | 3² = 9 |
| 7 × 7 | 2² = 4 |
| 8 × 8 | 1² = 1 |
| **Total** | **204** |

## The general formula

The total is the sum of the first eight perfect squares, and there's a well-known formula for the sum of the first n squares:

1² + 2² + 3² + ... + n² = n(n + 1)(2n + 1) / 6

With n = 8, this gives (8 × 9 × 17) / 6 = 1,224 / 6 = 204, matching the table. The formula works for any square grid. A 3 × 3 tic-tac-toe board, for example, has 9 + 4 + 1 = 14 squares.

## Going further: rectangles

The puzzle is sometimes extended to rectangles. Every rectangle on the board is defined by picking two of the 9 horizontal grid lines and two of the 9 vertical grid lines. There are C(9, 2) = 36 ways to choose each pair, so the board contains 36 × 36 = **1,296** rectangles, 204 of which are squares.

## Summary

- **64** individual squares
- **204** squares of all sizes
- **1,296** rectangles of all sizes, squares included

The question is a classic precisely because most people stop at 64. For a complete answer, say which interpretation you're using and show the sum that leads to 204.

The Office on the Fourteenth Floor

Dr. Eleanor Vance maintained her practice in an unremarkable building downtown, between a dental surgery and an accounting firm. Her nameplate listed no specialty. Referrals arrived by word of mouth, through channels that she had learned not to question.

Her nine o'clock on Monday was a man who had once attempted to flood a coastal city. He sat in the armchair across from her, removed his gloves with deliberate care, and spoke for forty minutes about his father.

"He told me the ocean would take everything eventually," the man said. "I suppose I wished to prove him right on my own schedule."

Dr. Vance made a note. She did not write the word *villain* in her files. She had abandoned that term early in her career, after realizing it described an outcome rather than a person. Her clients had committed terrible acts; several remained capable of committing more. Her work was not to absolve them. It was to understand what had brought them to the threshold, and whether any of them might still be persuaded to step back.

At eleven, a young woman who called herself the Archivist arrived twelve minutes late and apologized four times. She had erased the memories of an entire town in pursuit of what she described as a cleaner history. In session, she was meticulous, anxious, and frightened of being forgotten herself. Dr. Vance observed, not for the first time, that grandiose ambitions frequently concealed very small and very old fears.

"Do you believe I can change?" the Archivist asked.

"I believe you are asking," Dr. Vance replied, "and that is not nothing."

Her afternoon client was the most difficult. He had no particular grievance, no wounded childhood that he would admit to, and no stated objective beyond what he termed "the elegance of collapse." He found the therapeutic process amusing and treated each session as a game of chess in which he was several moves ahead.

"You know what I am," he said. "Why continue?"

Dr. Vance considered the question with the seriousness it deserved. "Because you continue to come," she said. "No one compels you. Some part of you wants something from this room. I am patient enough to wait until you can tell me what it is."

He was silent for a long moment. Then he looked at the clock and stood. "Same time next week," he said, which was the closest he had ever come to an answer.

In the evenings, Dr. Vance wrote her case notes and then consulted with her own supervisor, a retired psychiatrist who reminded her, regularly, of the ethical limits of confidentiality and of her duty to warn when lives were at stake. She had invoked that duty twice. Both clients had returned afterward, which surprised her each time.

She did not consider herself brave. She considered herself a professional who had accepted an unusual caseload. Every person, she had come to believe, was the protagonist of their own account, however distorted. Her task was to sit with that account long enough to locate the first wrong turn.

Occasionally, she found it. Occasionally, the client turned back.

Those were the days she remembered, and the reason she kept the office on the fourteenth floor.

Convolutional neural networks owe much of their success on images to the regular grid structure and translation symmetry of the plane, neither of which exists on curved surfaces. A common workaround maps a surface to a planar domain and applies a standard CNN, but existing surface-to-image representations either introduce large area distortion or require several images to cover the whole shape. We propose a new representation for sphere-type surfaces based on general covering maps. Rather than relying on a toric cover with a fixed set of cone points, our construction lets a flat torus wrap around the surface several times, so that every region appears with low distortion somewhere in a single image. Because this image is seamless and periodic, convolution with circular padding is well defined, and off-the-shelf architectures apply with minimal modification. Predictions from the multiple copies of each surface point are then aggregated back onto the mesh. Experiments on shape segmentation and classification benchmarks show that the method matches or exceeds competing approaches while remaining simple and efficient.

Pop Culture Roundup: "Star Wars" Fans Get a Jolt, and a Reporter's Rant Goes Viral for All the Wrong Reasons

It was a week of extremes in entertainment news, with one long-awaited trailer sending fans into a frenzy and one short video clip sending a television reporter into damage-control mode. Here's a look at the stories that dominated conversation online.

**Han Solo is back**

The biggest moment of the week arrived when Lucasfilm unveiled the second teaser trailer for "Star Wars: The Force Awakens" at the Star Wars Celebration fan convention in Anaheim, California. Within hours, the two-minute preview had racked up millions of views and become the top trending topic on social media.

The trailer offered fleeting glimpses of new characters played by John Boyega, Daisy Ridley and Oscar Isaac, along with the wreckage of a Star Destroyer half-buried in desert sand. But the shot that sent fans over the edge came at the very end, when Harrison Ford appeared as Han Solo alongside Chewbacca and delivered a single line: "Chewie, we're home."

Fans who packed the convention hall reportedly screamed so loudly when Ford appeared that the audio was hard to hear. Director J.J. Abrams and producer Kathleen Kennedy took the stage to introduce the footage and were joined by members of the cast, including original stars Mark Hamill and Carrie Fisher.

The film, the first installment in a new trilogy, is scheduled to open in December.

**An apology after a meltdown**

On the other end of the spectrum, ESPN reporter Britt McHenry found herself at the center of a backlash after a video surfaced showing her berating an employee at a towing company in Virginia.

In the footage, which was recorded by a security camera and posted online, McHenry can be heard insulting the woman's appearance, education and job, telling her she was "on television" while the employee was not. The clip spread quickly, drawing widespread criticism from viewers who called her comments cruel and elitist.

ESPN announced that McHenry had been suspended for one week. McHenry apologized on Twitter, writing that she had allowed her emotions to get the better of her during "an intense and stressful moment" and that she was "embarrassed" by her behavior.

The episode set off a broader online debate about how people treat service workers, as well as how much a private moment caught on camera should affect someone's career.

**Elsewhere in entertainment**

The week also brought plenty of smaller buzz. Streaming services continued their push for original programming, a handful of networks announced which shows had been renewed or canceled ahead of the fall season, and festival lineups for the summer concert circuit continued to roll out, giving music fans plenty to plan around.

If this week proved anything, it's that the internet can turn a two-minute video into a global event, whether that video features a beloved space smuggler or a moment someone would surely rather forget.

**Boko Haram Pledges Allegiance to ISIS, but Analyst Sees Little Immediate Battlefield Change**

The Nigerian militant group Boko Haram has reportedly pledged its allegiance to ISIS, a move that formally links one of Africa's deadliest insurgencies with the extremist organization controlling large parts of Iraq and Syria.

The pledge appeared in an audio message attributed to Boko Haram leader Abubakar Shekau and posted online. In the recording, the speaker declares loyalty to ISIS leader Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi. The authenticity of the message could not be independently verified, though it follows months of growing signs that the two groups were moving closer, including increasingly similar propaganda and video production.

Boko Haram has waged a violent campaign in northeastern Nigeria for years, killing thousands of people and displacing well over a million. The group drew worldwide condemnation in 2014 after kidnapping more than 200 schoolgirls from the town of Chibok. In recent months, its attacks have spilled into neighboring Cameroon, Niger, and Chad, prompting a regional military offensive.

Despite the dramatic headline, at least one expert cautions against overstating the immediate significance. J. Peter Pham, director of the Atlantic Council's Africa Center, said that in the short term the alliance is unlikely to have a major impact on the battlefield. Boko Haram's fighters, tactics, and areas of operation will remain largely the same, and the two groups are separated by vast distances that make sharing fighters or weapons difficult.

Pham suggested that the pledge is more about branding and legitimacy. For Boko Haram, which is under mounting military pressure, aligning with ISIS could boost its profile and help with recruitment. For ISIS, the pledge offers a chance to claim expansion into West Africa.

Over the longer term, analysts warn, closer ties could bring Boko Haram greater access to funding, expertise, and propaganda resources, a development that would deepen concern among governments in the region and beyond.

Let T and S be commuting contractions on a Hilbert space H. A vector x is called a joint coboundary if it lies in the range of both I − T and I − S, and a double coboundary if it lies in the range of (I − T)(I − S). Every double coboundary is clearly a joint coboundary, and we study when the converse holds. We show that, in general, the inclusion is strict: there exist commuting unitary operators, and even commuting contractions arising from measure-preserving actions, for which some joint coboundaries fail to be double coboundaries. On the other hand, we obtain sufficient conditions, expressed through spectral properties and the closedness of the relevant ranges, under which the two notions coincide. Applications to the joint behavior of ergodic averages and to the solvability of coupled cohomological equations are discussed.

Data observed in complex systems frequently exhibit non-Gaussian features, such as heavy tails, skewness, and abrupt jumps, that are poorly captured by models driven by Brownian noise. This paper develops a framework for quantifying model uncertainty when observations are non-Gaussian, using the Hellinger distance as a measure of discrepancy between the probability distribution generated by a candidate stochastic model and that of the observed data. We consider stochastic differential equations driven by α-stable Lévy noise and derive the evolution of their probability densities through the associated nonlocal Fokker–Planck equations. The Hellinger distance between model and data densities is then minimized to estimate unknown parameters and to select the most plausible model. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the approach accurately identifies noise parameters and distinguishes Gaussian from non-Gaussian dynamics, providing a practical tool for data-driven modeling under uncertainty.

Machete-Wielding Suspect in New Orleans Airport Attack Dies; Sheriff Says Bag Held Molotov Cocktails and Smoke Bombs

NEW ORLEANS — The man accused of charging into a security checkpoint at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport with a machete has died after being shot by a sheriff's deputy, authorities said, as investigators revealed he had also been carrying an arsenal of homemade incendiary devices.

Richard White, 63, died at a hospital where he had been treated for gunshot wounds sustained during the confrontation Friday night, according to the Jefferson Parish Sheriff's Office. He had been taken into surgery shortly after the attack and remained in critical condition before succumbing to his injuries.

Jefferson Parish Sheriff Newell Normand told reporters that a search of White's belongings turned up six Molotov cocktails, several smoke bombs and other materials. The sheriff said the contents of the bag suggested the attack may have been planned, though investigators had not yet determined a motive.

"This individual came prepared to do harm," Normand said at a news conference. "What he intended to do with those devices, we may never fully know."

According to the sheriff's account, White approached a checkpoint operated by the Transportation Security Administration at around 8 p.m. He allegedly sprayed a TSA officer with what appeared to be a can of wasp and insect spray before pulling out a machete and chasing screening officers through the area. Travelers waiting in line scattered as officers ran for cover.

A Jefferson Parish deputy stationed nearby responded within moments. The deputy fired three shots, striking White in the face, chest and thigh, Normand said. A TSA officer was also struck in the arm by one of the rounds and was treated at a hospital for a non-life-threatening wound. A second TSA employee suffered minor injuries during the chaos.

Witnesses described a frightening scene. One passenger said she heard screaming and saw people running toward the gates before hearing gunshots. "Everybody just dropped," she said. "Nobody knew what was happening."

The concourse was evacuated and several flights were delayed as police secured the area and bomb technicians examined White's bag. Operations gradually resumed later that night.

Investigators said White had no significant criminal history. Neighbors and acquaintances in the New Orleans suburb of Kenner, where he lived, described him as a quiet man. Officials said they were looking into his medical and personal background as part of the inquiry. Authorities said there was no indication that he was acting with anyone else or that the attack was connected to any terrorist organization.

The sheriff praised the deputy's quick reaction, saying the response likely prevented further injuries in a crowded terminal. "In a matter of seconds, he made the decision that needed to be made," Normand said.

The TSA said in a statement that it was grateful for the swift action of law enforcement and that its officers had followed their training. The agency added that it was reviewing the incident with airport and local officials.

The attack renewed questions about the vulnerability of public areas of airports that sit before security screening, where travelers gather in large numbers. The FBI is assisting the sheriff's office with the investigation.

This phenomenon reflects several well-documented features of human memory and cognition. First, memory consolidation continues after practice has ended; during rest, and particularly during sleep, the brain reorganizes and strengthens newly acquired information, integrating it with existing knowledge. Second, the spacing effect demonstrates that learning distributed over time produces more durable understanding than concentrated study, partly because retrieving partially forgotten material requires effort that reinforces it. Third, stepping away reduces mental fatigue and allows the mind to abandon unproductive approaches, a process sometimes termed incubation. When one returns, the problem can be viewed afresh, without the fixation that previously obstructed progress. Finally, the brain's unconscious processing may continue to make connections while attention is directed elsewhere. Collectively, these mechanisms explain why a period of rest frequently yields clearer and deeper comprehension.

**Rosberg Leads Mercedes One-Two in Melbourne Practice as Vettel Impresses for Ferrari**

MELBOURNE, Australia — Nico Rosberg set the pace in practice for the Australian Grand Prix on Friday, edging out Mercedes teammate Lewis Hamilton and signaling that the Silver Arrows remain the team to beat as the new Formula One season gets underway.

Rosberg's lap at Albert Park put him at the top of the timesheets, with the reigning world champion Hamilton close behind. The result will come as little surprise to rivals who watched the German manufacturer dominate last year, when Rosberg and Hamilton combined to win all but three of the season's 19 races.

The early evidence suggests that advantage has not disappeared over the winter. Both Mercedes drivers looked comfortable throughout the session, and other teams will be hoping the gap narrows once qualifying begins on Saturday.

The brightest note for the chasing pack came from Sebastian Vettel. The four-time world champion, beginning his first season with Ferrari after leaving Red Bull, finished third in the second practice session. It was an encouraging start for both the driver and the Italian team, which endured a winless and difficult campaign last year.

Away from the track, the weekend has been overshadowed by a legal dispute at Sauber. Giedo van der Garde, who says he held a valid contract to race for the Swiss team this season, won a court ruling in Melbourne supporting his claim to a seat. Despite that ruling, the Dutchman did not take part in practice, and Sauber ran its two other contracted drivers instead. The standoff between the team and van der Garde remains unresolved, and further legal action is possible before Sunday's race.

With qualifying still to come, Rosberg's pace offers an early indication that the championship fight may once again be a contest between the two Mercedes drivers.

# Maine Wild Food Survival Guide

## The Golden Rules

1. **Never eat what you can't identify with total certainty.** One mistake with a mushroom or a wild carrot lookalike can kill you.
2. **Fat and protein matter more than greens.** Lean meat alone (rabbit, especially) leads to "rabbit starvation." Seek fat: beaver tail, nuts, fish, bone marrow.
3. **Boil all water.** Giardia lives in even the clearest brook.
4. **Think in seasons.** Maine gives freely from May to October, then becomes stingy. Store food all summer.

## Plants and Greens

**Cattail** (marshes, pond edges) is the single most useful plant in Maine. Spring shoots taste like cucumber when peeled. Green flower heads can be boiled and eaten like corn. Rhizomes yield starch all year, even under ice.

**Fiddleheads** (ostrich fern, May) grow along river floodplains. Choose only those with a smooth stem and a deep U-shaped groove on the inside, like celery. Always boil them for 10+ minutes; raw ones cause illness.

**Dandelion, chickweed, lamb's quarters, plantain, purslane, and wood sorrel** are common, safe, and full of vitamins. Dandelion roots can be roasted in fall.

**Seaweed** along the coast is abundant and nutritious: dulse, kelp, Irish moss, and rockweed. Glasswort (sea beans) grows in salt marshes and is salty and crisp.

**Pine and spruce:** inner bark (cambium) is edible in an emergency, and needle tea provides vitamin C through winter. Avoid yew, which has flat, soft needles and red berries. It is deadly.

## Fruits and Nuts

- **Lowbush blueberries** (July–August) cover barrens and burned ground. Dry them in the sun for winter.
- **Wild strawberries** (June), **raspberries and blackberries** (July–August)
- **Cranberries** in bogs (September–October); they keep for weeks.
- **Chokecherries and pin cherries:** eat the flesh, spit the pits (they contain cyanide compounds).
- **Rose hips** last into winter and are rich in vitamin C.
- **Beechnuts, hazelnuts, and butternuts** are high in fat.
- **Acorns** are plentiful but bitter. Crack them, then soak or boil in changes of water until the bitterness is gone. Grind into flour.

## Fungi

Learn a few and learn them perfectly.

- **Chanterelles** (summer, hardwoods): golden, with blunt false ridges that run down the stem. Jack-o'-lantern mushrooms are orange, grow in clusters on wood, and have true sharp gills.
- **Chicken of the woods:** bright orange-yellow shelves on dead oak. Unmistakable.
- **Oyster mushrooms:** fan-shaped, on dead hardwood, nearly year-round.
- **Hen of the woods:** large gray clusters at the base of oaks in fall.
- **Giant puffballs:** slice them top to bottom. The inside must be pure white with no outline of a mushroom shape (that would be a deadly Amanita button).
- **Morels** (spring): fully hollow inside. False morels are cottony or chambered inside.

Never eat any white-gilled mushroom. The destroying angel grows across Maine.

## Animals

**Big game:** white-tailed deer and moose provide hundreds of pounds of meat. Use every part: hide, sinew, bone, and fat.

**Small game:** snowshoe hare and squirrels are easy to snare along trails. Ruffed grouse can often be knocked down with a thrown stick. Porcupines move slowly and can be killed with a club, which makes them a classic emergency food. Beaver is fatty and abundant in nearly every watershed.

**Wild turkey** are common in southern and central Maine.

**Fish:** brook trout fill cold streams. In spring, alewives and smelt run upriver in huge numbers and can be scooped by hand or net. Ice fishing sustains you through winter.

**Shellfish:** soft-shell clams on mudflats, blue mussels on rocks, and periwinkles in tide pools. Lobsters can be caught in shallow water with simple traps. Be aware of red tide: shellfish can carry paralytic toxins in warm months. If you eat a small portion and your lips tingle, stop immediately.

**Insects and grubs** are reliable protein when all else fails. Cook them first.

## Deadly Plants to Know

- **Water hemlock:** grows in wet areas, white umbrella flowers, purple-streaked stems, chambered root. The most toxic plant in North America.
- **Poison hemlock:** similar look, with a musty smell and purple blotches.
- **Baneberry:** white or red berries on stalks. Toxic.
- **Any white umbrella-flowered plant** (carrot family): avoid entirely unless you are an expert.

## Seasonal Plan

- **Spring:** fiddleheads, shoots, fish runs, morels
- **Summer:** berries, greens, shellfish, mushrooms
- **Fall:** nuts, roots, cranberries, hunting, smoking and drying meat
- **Winter:** stored food, ice fishing, snaring, cattail roots, needle tea

Preserve everything you can. In Maine, winter decides who survives.

The first person to notice was a barber named Elias Moreno, which made sense, because nobody spends more time watching mirrors than barbers.

He was trimming the back of Mr. Hollis's neck on a Tuesday morning when he glanced up and saw his reflection holding the scissors a half-second late. Not much. Just a lag, like a video call on a bad connection. Elias stopped. His reflection stopped a beat after him.

He blinked. His reflection blinked, eventually.

"Something wrong?" said Mr. Hollis.

"No," said Elias, and kept cutting, and did not look up again for the rest of the day.

By Thursday it was everywhere. People filmed themselves waving at bathroom mirrors and posted the clips with confused captions. The delay was growing. Half a second became a full second, then two. Scientists went on the news with careful faces and said words like "optical anomaly" and "under investigation," which everyone understood to mean they had no idea.

What none of them knew, what nobody on this side had ever known, was that mirrors were not reflecting anything. They were windows. On the other side lived another Earth, a perfect copy with left and right swapped, where another Elias cut another Mr. Hollis's hair in another shop with the barber pole on the other side of the door. For all of history, the two worlds had moved in perfect lockstep, every gesture matched, every glance returned. There had never been a reason to suspect anything.

Until something on the other side slipped.

Nobody would ever learn exactly what. Maybe a single atom decayed when its twin didn't. Maybe a butterfly in the mirror-Amazon flapped its wings counterclockwise. Whatever it was, the two worlds had begun to drift apart, and the drift was accelerating.

By the second week, the delay was gone, replaced by something worse: divergence. People looked into mirrors and saw themselves doing things they weren't doing. A woman in Ohio watched her reflection brush its teeth while she stood perfectly still, toothbrush in hand. A teenager in Seoul saw his reflection get up and walk out of frame, leaving an empty bedroom behind the glass.

Elias kept the shop open, because people still needed haircuts, but he hung sheets over the mirrors. Customers didn't complain. Most of them had done the same at home.

One evening, after closing, he lifted the corner of the sheet. He couldn't help it.

His reflection was sitting in the barber chair, facing him. It looked tired. It had a few days of stubble that Elias didn't have, and its shop was messier, the floor unswept. It held up a piece of paper, the handwriting backward, and Elias had to read it twice.

YOU SEE IT TOO?

Elias grabbed a pen from the counter and wrote on the back of a receipt, slowly, in mirror letters, the way he'd practiced as a kid for fun: YES.

His reflection laughed. Elias had never seen himself laugh from the outside before. It was a strange sound to see without hearing.

They talked for hours that way, holding paper to the glass. The other Elias said his world was frightened too. Their scientists also had careful faces. Their mirrors were also covered in sheets.

DO YOU THINK IT STOPS? the other Elias wrote.

Elias thought about it. He thought about all the years he'd spent looking into mirrors, never once imagining someone was looking back.

I DON'T KNOW, he wrote. BUT COME BACK TOMORROW.

The next night, the other Elias was waiting. So was he. And as the two worlds kept drifting, two barbers kept meeting at the glass, holding up their backward letters, trying to stay in sync on purpose.

**Halcyon**

They called it Halcyon, and for nineteen days it was the best thing that had ever happened to the world.

On the twentieth day, the first recipients didn't wake up. By the end of the month, the ones who hadn't died had started screaming, and not at random. In the last week anyone was still broadcasting, the anchors made a point of it: the afflicted screamed at windows, at spoons, at the black glass of switched-off phones. At anything that could hold a reflection.

I got my dose the first morning, in a folding chair in a high school gym. The nurse gave me a sticker shaped like a yellow sun. I remember thinking I was lucky.

I still think so, mostly. I haven't died. I haven't screamed. For six weeks I've walked through a silent city, stepping around broken glass, telling myself that whatever took everyone else simply missed me, the way lightning misses most people.

But I've been careful. I shave by feel. I taped a towel over the bathroom mirror the day my neighbor put her head through hers.

This morning, I pulled the towel down.

My face was there. Thinner, unshaven, eyes bloodshot from bad sleep, but mine. I almost laughed. I lifted a hand to touch the stubble on my jaw, and the man in the mirror lifted his.

A fraction of a second late.

I went still. He went still too, a heartbeat after me, and we studied each other for a long time. That was when I understood what the others had seen. Not a monster. Nothing so simple. Just patience: the calm, attentive look of something that had spent six weeks practicing being me.

Slowly, I lowered my hand.

He didn't.

Space Exploration or Problems on Earth?

Today many countries spend a lot of money for space exploration. They send rockets to the Moon and to Mars, and they build big telescopes. But some people think this money should be use to solve problems on Earth, like poverty, hunger and climate change. In my opinion, both are important, but governments should spend more money on Earth problems first.

First, there are many people in the world who don't have enough food or clean water. In some countries, children cannot go to school because their family is too poor. When I see this on the news, I feel very sad. I think it is strange that we spend billions of dollars to go to Mars while some peoples are dying from hunger. If governments use this money for hospitals, schools and clean water, many lifes can be saved.

Second, our planet has a lot of environment problems. The climate is changing and the weather become more extreme every year. We have floods, fires and very hot summers. Scientists say we need to act fast. I believe protecting Earth is more urgent than exploring other planets, because Earth is the only home we have right now.

However, I also understand why space exploration is useful. Many technology we use every day came from space research. For example, GPS, weather satellites and some medical equipments were developed because of space programs. Satellites also help us to watch the climate change and to predict storms. So space exploration is not only about going to other planets, it can help people on Earth too.

Also, space exploration makes young people interested in science. When I was child, I watched a video about astronauts and I wanted to become one. Maybe space programs can inspire students to study hard and become scientists or engineers in the future.

In conclusion, I think governments should not stop space exploration completely, because it gives us useful technology and inspiration. But they should spend most of money on solving problems on Earth, like hunger, poverty and the environment. If we take care of our planet first, then we can explore space with more better conditions. A good balance is the best answer for this question.

They knew.

Thanksgiving at my aunt Carol's house always began the same way: the smell of turkey that had been in the oven since dawn, the football game muttering in the den, my cousins arguing about who got the good chair. This year the smells and sounds were the same, but the moment I stepped into the foyer, every conversation stopped for exactly one heartbeat too long.

"Danny!" Aunt Carol said, with a smile that didn't reach anywhere near her eyes. "You made it."

"I made it," I said.

She hugged me with the stiff tenderness of someone holding a bomb.

I had told exactly one person. My mother. Three weeks ago, on the phone, after two glasses of wine and a long silence, I had said, "Mom, I quit law school." And she had said, after an even longer silence, "Okay. Okay. We'll talk about it." Then she had apparently talked about it with everyone in the tri-state area.

My uncle Ray clapped me on the shoulder. "How's school?" he asked, and then his eyes slid over to my mother, who was suddenly very interested in a dish of cranberry sauce.

"It's fine," I said.

My grandmother patted the seat next to her on the couch. "Sit, sweetheart. Tell me what you're doing these days." Her voice was gentle in the way you'd talk to a horse that might bolt.

I sat. Across the room, my cousin Megan, who had passed the bar exam on her first try and never let anyone forget it, gave me a look of such enormous sympathy that I wanted to crawl under the carpet.

For two hours it went on like this. Nobody said it. Everyone circled it. Uncle Ray told a story about a friend's son who "found his passion" after "a few false starts." My aunt mentioned, apropos of nothing, that "plenty of successful people changed direction." My grandfather, who was eighty-nine and mostly deaf, said loudly, "Is this the one who flunked out?" and the room went silent until Carol announced the rolls were ready.

I didn't flunk out. I left. There's a difference, though I wasn't sure anyone at that table would hear it.

When we finally sat down to eat, my mother caught my eye. She looked miserable. I realized she hadn't been gossiping, or not only gossiping. She had been asking for help. She had been asking everyone what to say to me, because she didn't know.

I put my fork down.

"Okay," I said. "I quit law school."

The silence that followed was the purest silence I had ever heard in that house.

"I know you all know," I went on. "I'd rather just talk about it than have everyone tiptoe around me all night. I wasn't happy. I was good at it, but I wasn't happy. I'm working at a woodshop in Easton right now. I'm building furniture. I'm learning. And I'm okay."

Nobody moved. Then my grandfather, who had heard every word for once, said, "Furniture?"

"Furniture," I said.

He nodded slowly. "My father built furniture. Best man I ever knew."

And just like that, the room exhaled. Uncle Ray asked what kind of wood I liked working with. Megan admitted she hated her firm. My aunt asked if I could fix her wobbly dining chair, the one she'd been threatening to throw out for a decade.

My mother didn't say anything. She just reached under the table and squeezed my hand.

The glances were still there for the rest of the night, but they had changed. They weren't hooded anymore. They were curious. The smiles weren't practiced. They were real.

On my way out, Aunt Carol handed me a bag of leftovers and the wobbly chair.

"No pressure," she said.

I laughed, and for the first time all evening, so did she.

Obama pushed hard for fast-track authority (formally, Trade Promotion Authority) on the Trans-Pacific Partnership for a few interconnected reasons.

**Getting the deal done at all.** Fast-track lets Congress vote yes or no on a trade agreement without amending it. Other countries, especially Japan, were reluctant to make final concessions if Congress could later rewrite the terms. Without TPA, negotiators believed the TPP would likely collapse.

**Geopolitics and China.** The administration framed TPP as central to its "pivot to Asia." Obama argued that if the U.S. didn't help write the rules for trade in the Asia-Pacific, China would, on terms less favorable to American workers and businesses.

**Economic goals.** The deal would cut tariffs on U.S. exports, set standards for intellectual property and digital trade, and include labor and environmental provisions stronger than earlier agreements like NAFTA.

**Legacy.** TPP was a signature second-term initiative.

The push was notable because most opposition came from Obama's own party, so he worked with Republican leaders to pass TPA in 2015.

The two-dimensional electron system that forms at the interface between the band insulators LaAlO₃ and SrTiO₃ displays a remarkable variety of behavior, including gate-tunable superconductivity, signatures of magnetism, strong spin–orbit coupling and unusual magnetotransport. Whether these phenomena share a common microscopic origin has remained an open question. Here we present systematic magnetotransport measurements, performed as a function of gate-controlled carrier density, on a series of interfaces with different LaAlO₃ thicknesses and electron mobilities. In every sample we identify a critical density of approximately 1.7 × 10¹³ cm⁻², at which transport changes abruptly from single-carrier to multi-carrier behavior. This density is universal, independent of both layer thickness and mobility. The characteristics of the transition, together with its consistency with spectroscopic data, identify it as a Lifshitz transition at which electrons begin to occupy the heavier dxz/dyz bands in addition to the light dxy band. We further show that the same density marks the onset of strong spin–orbit interaction and anomalous magnetoresistance. These results point to orbital band filling as a unifying principle behind the emergent physics of this oxide interface.
